cells.tense: You are standing in the thing that got built, and the pen is in your hand.
cells.ask: Say out loud what you finished and that it was you who finished it. Then go on with the day.
cells.core:
You're standing in what you finished, and the pen is still in your hand. People who might not say it see the thing standing there, and the room you walk through quietly holds what you made. You chose it and you carried it to the end, which is why it's here.

The part that's easy to skip: saying it's yours. Not loud, not to anyone in particular. You can keep doing the work — the next thing is already there — but finish the count while the structure still stands. What this balance is free to feed next is patience with where you actually are. Name what got finished. It costs a few seconds and guards the thing from being treated as ordinary.

cells.verb: finish what you started and let it stand

cells.tense: You will have finished it a hundred times in your head before anyone has seen anything.
cells.ask: Before you change anything, stop — wait until the thing has been finished for three days before you touch it again.
cells.core:
You're running past the end. In your head it's already done, already admired, already the start of what comes after — so you keep finishing it, again and again, before anyone has seen the standing thing. The work is faster than the moment it makes. Someone says it's done and you hear a beginning.

That's the pushing: it keeps the ground from setting. You know how to hold a thing to the end, and right now that holding has nowhere to land, so it eats the day it just won. Leave the thing in the room for three days. Not deciding, not starting. Let what is actually finished be finished. What shows up in that quiet is closer to the next thing than any plan you'll force.

cells.tense: Something in you went quiet after a certain room, and you have not built much since.
cells.ask: Choose one thing you can finish in a day and finish it — something that stays put when the day is out.
cells.core:
Not much of yours is standing anywhere — not because you lost the ability to build, but because the work got left in the same room. You know what a finished thing feels like, and some part of you has been standing outside since. So new building is hard to start now. The days move. The shelf stays empty.

One small thing brought to a real end can loosen that. Sweep one room completely and look at it before you leave — not the whole place, a small area you can see done in a day, closed and kept. That might tell you what the quiet has been protecting. Then do the small thing anyway, while you still don't know. That's the moving through.

cells.tense: You are writing your own account of this place and calling it the account of events.
cells.ask: Say out loud, to no one in particular: 'I did this,' about one thing in the room within arm's reach.
cells.core:
You make the day go, and you know the day goes, but you talk about the doing like it's water that finds its own way down. The work gets done. The room runs because your hand is on it. But you describe afternoons as something that happened to you, which means the one person who keeps the structure standing gets credited to the structure.

It doesn't need a ceremony. Pick one thing within reach — anything that you made or moved or decided — and own it flat: 'I did this.' Then stop. Not because the standing needs praise. Because when the hands don't get their name back, the work starts to feel like it belongs to no one, and it stops teaching you what you actually are.
